nameStory: Common arrowgrass gets its name from its distinctive fruit that splits into pointed segments resembling tiny arrowheads. When the seeds are ripe, these arrow-shaped pieces break away and can pierce soft surfaces, giving the plant its memorable common name. The scientific name 'Triglochin' literally means 'three points' in Greek, referring to these characteristic three-pointed fruits.
description: Common arrowgrass is a slender, grass-like perennial that grows in dense clumps in salty or brackish wetlands. Despite its name, it's not actually a true grass but belongs to its own unique family. The plant produces narrow, fleshy leaves that arise directly from the base and can reach 1-2 feet tall. Tiny greenish flowers appear on tall, spike-like stems above the foliage, later developing into the characteristic arrow-shaped fruits.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - small fruits that split into 3-6 pointed segments resembling tiny arrowheads, giving the plant its name

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, fleshy, grass-like leaves that feel slightly succulent and arise directly from the base in dense tufts

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers arranged in long, narrow spikes on leafless stems that extend above the foliage

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps or colonies in wet areas, with all leaves emerging from ground level in a bunch-grass pattern

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel distinctly thick and fleshy when rolled between fingers, unlike the thin, dry texture of true grasses

habitat: Look for common arrowgrass in salt marshes, brackish wetlands, and occasionally freshwater marshes along New England's coast. It thrives in areas that flood regularly with salt or brackish water, often growing alongside saltmarsh cordgrass and other salt-tolerant plants. You might also find it in inland alkaline wetlands and fens where groundwater is mineral-rich.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the base, bright green and succulent-looking. Plants begin their active growing season as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs with tall spikes of tiny greenish blooms rising above the foliage. This is the best time to see the distinctive flower arrangement.
seasonality.fall: Fruits mature and split into the characteristic arrow-shaped segments. Seeds disperse and leaves may begin to yellow or brown.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to underground parts in harsh climates, though some leaves may persist in milder coastal areas.

funFact: Common arrowgrass is one of the few plants that can actually tolerate being completely submerged in salt water during high tides - it has special adaptations that allow it to excrete excess salt through its leaves, making tiny salt crystals visible on the leaf surfaces on sunny days.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with true salt marsh grasses, but the fleshy, succulent-feeling leaves are a dead giveaway - true grasses have thin, flat, or rolled leaves that feel dry and papery. Remember: if it feels juicy like a tiny succulent, it's probably arrowgrass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, arrowgrass isn't a grass at all but belongs to an ancient plant family that's more closely related to water lilies than to true grasses. This naming confusion is common with many grass-like plants that aren't actually grasses.
compareHints: Common arrowgrass is much more widespread than its rare relative, Gaspé Peninsula arrowgrass, which is found only in a few locations in northern New England. Common arrowgrass typically has 6-ribbed fruits while Gaspé Peninsula arrowgrass has 3-ribbed fruits, though both split into arrow-shaped segments. If you're seeing arrowgrass in a salt marsh or common wetland, it's almost certainly the common species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Gaspé Peninsula Arrowgrass is much smaller and rarer than its relative, common arrowgrass, which grows taller and is more widespread.
